title: LLM for Public Data: Generating Synthetic Personas for Population Analysis
summary: This platform uses an LLM to generate statistically accurate synthetic personas from public data, allowing policy researchers and business strategists to model entire populations who are poorly represented in standard AI training data.
domain: It really can be used for multiple use cases.
beneficiaries: Policy researchers, data scientists, and business strategists who need to understand, model, and serve populations (e.g., low-income or rural households) that are poorly represented in standard, web-based LLM training data.
geoScope: Global. It currently has U.S. data in the tool.
deploymentStage: Pilot / Limited Deployment: In use with a specific partner or limited user group.
aiModel: We use a proprietary model built on a Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuned for querying and analyzing structured public datasets.
barriers: Primary barriers include: (1) Building trust with public sector and academic users who are accustomed to manual data extraction. (2) Sourcing and integrating the vast array of relevant international public datasets to expand the tool's geographic scope beyond the U.S.
enablers: A strategic partnership with a federal agency or a multinational body to serve as a pilot partner. This would provide access to key datasets and build the credibility needed for wider adoption.

beneficiaries: This benefits anyone interested in the history of the forced internment of over 120,000 Japanese Americans during World War II.

deploymentStage: Broadly Deployed: Widely available and in active use.

aiModel: The creator used Hailuo and Kling video generators and the voices in this film are real. They come from survivors, their families, and historians, collected through interviews and documentaries.

title: Smarter, greener mineral exploration using AI
summary: For exploration teams, regulators, and host communities, this AI technology fuses geology, geophysics, and remote-sensing data to pinpoint high-probability deposits—cutting guesswork, drilling, costs, and environmental disturbance.
beneficiaries: Communities living near prospective copper and lithium deposits—especially in the African Copperbelt—who face the greatest environmental disturbance from exploration.
geoScope: Zambia’s Copperbelt (Mingomba project near Chililabombwe), with pilot studies in Québec and Australia—expanding globally.
deploymentStage: Pilot / Limited Deployment: In use with a specific partner or limited user group.
evidence: A Copperbelt exploration team using the AI platform re-ranked legacy targets with newly digitized 1950s-era maps; the system prioritized deeper structures that prior campaigns had overlooked, leading to the Mingomba drill hits and a faster path to mine planning—reducing unnecessary holes and footprint versus “grid-drill everything.” See https://koboldmetals.com/ and https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/kobold-metals-ai-copper-lithium-caad58da and https://www.ted.com/talks/mfikeyi_makayi_the_emerging_science_of_finding_critical_metals?autoplay=true
aiModel: A proprietary, multimodal AI system that combines rock/soil data and geophysical surveys with satellite and field photos to make a probability map of the best places to drill. It uses multiple models, shows how confident it is, and keeps learning from old maps and every new drill result in each region.
barriers: Fragmented data: Incomplete/uneven legacy maps and proprietary surveys limit training and transfer.  Capital risk: High upfront cost for AI + new surveys with uncertain returns.  Permitting & data rules: Slow approvals and data-sovereignty constraints impede sharing and validation.
enablers:
Open up the maps and data. Governments and survey agencies should share old geology maps, drill results, and geophysics in easy-to-use, standard formats so AI tools can learn faster.

Create joint funds (public + private) that help pay for early AI-guided surveys and drilling, in return for clear environmental reporting and benefits for local communities.

title: Prevention of human-caused catastrophes (HumCat)
summary: The KOS employs a combination of methods to capture preventions, including behavioral analytics, language models and rules-based neurosymbolic AI
beneficiaries: Human-caused catastrophes typically impact the least fortunate communities the most
geoScope: Globally with primary focus on U.S.
deploymentStage: Pilot / Limited Deployment: In use with a specific partner or limited user group.
evidence: We can't yet prove it yet but nearly three decades of R&D is convincing. We have done deep-dives on many, including the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. In addition to 11 lives list, theJanuary 2018 Journal of Corporate Accounting & Finance 29(1):69-79 DOI:10.1002/jcaf.22306 -- estimates total costs of just under $150 billion.  Other estimates to BP alone are $71B https://www.nola.com/news/business/bp-and-its-partners-have-spent-71-billion-over-10-years-on-deepwater-horizon-disaster/article_ca773cc0-80f4-11ea-8fbe-ffa77e5297bd.html
aiModel: We developed the KOS from the theorem stage (1997). It's a complex adaptive system that employs a combination of proprietary methods, open source infrastructure, and data standards. For language model functionality we provide a menu of models and apply to specific functions according to strengths and weaknesses.
barriers: Primarily financial. We pioneered the HumCat model -- a ILS cat bond, which would have helped greatly but the costs for the technology and the bonds are non-trivial. Natcat bonds typically require sponsors.
enablers: Our KOS has 10 functions -- captured preventions being only one. If we could find a good public-private partnership specifically for Humcat prevention, and the first was demonstrated, our research suggests it would scale rapidly. We did have interest from several large institutional investors in HumCat bonds, but haven't found gap funding (low 7 figures).

title: Library-Augmented Generation (LAG)
summary: An LLM entryway that routes patrons to authoritative library sources via vector search and direct, citable links—no hallucinations, library values first.
beneficiaries: College students, faculty, librarians, archivists, historical researchers
geoScope: At Northwestern University Libraries in Boston, MA
deploymentStage: Pilot / Limited Deployment: In use with a specific partner or limited user group.
evidence: Early faculty demos describe the setup as a way to incorporate AI while preserving scholarly practices—relief that AI complements, not replaces, research. Queries are routed to library holdings with direct links (open and licensed), yielding “100% non-hallucinated” sources and encouraging users to read/verify the works themselves. fter adding museum connectors (Met, Art Institute of Chicago), the team can disable web RAG in tests and still return strong, collection-grounded answers on topics like Cubism—“very promising” results. See https://newsletter.dancohen.org/archive/the-librarys-new-entryway/ and https://newsletter.dancohen.org/archive/the-index-and-the-vector/ .
aiModel: A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server + Claude plugin enables what Cohen calls “library-augmented generation (LAG).
barriers: Wider use is slowed by content licenses and strict vendor rules, privacy laws that require careful handling of patron data, and security risks like prompt injection. It’s also hard to connect the system to many library tools (catalogs, link resolvers, museum/archives systems). Costs add up for hosting, vector search, and API calls. Some users don’t trust AI yet, so clear citations and training are needed. Accessibility and multilingual support must be strong. Schools also need clear ownership, approvals, and simple success metrics. Finally, AI models change often, so we need versioning and regular tests to keep quality steady.
enablers: Two things would help most: first, open and vendor-neutral ways to connect LLMs to library and museum collections—simple, standard APIs and licenses that allow retrieval and linking without letting content be used to train models, with clear logs for accountability. Second, consortial funding to build a shared, open-source toolkit (connectors, vector indexes, evaluation, accessibility/multilingual support) and to run pilots across many libraries so they can measure impact and improve together.

title: Decentralized infrastructure that makes AI training data verifiable and grounded in human participation versus blind consent.
summary: A provenance-driven data infrastructure that allows institutions to understand where training data comes from, how it was collected, and how it shapes model behaviour — enabling safer, fairer, and more accountable AI systems.
beneficiaries:
Researchers and model developers who need transparent, well-documented datasets.

Regulators and policymakers tasked with assessing whether AI systems meet safety, legality, and provenance standards.

Public institutions using AI in high-impact areas such as health, finance, and education.

Individuals and communities whose data underpins modern AI and who currently lack visibility or control.
deploymentStage: Broadly Deployed: Widely available and in active use.
evidence:
ODL-supported data networks have engaged over 1 million contributors, demonstrating that user-consented, provenance-tracked data can be collected at meaningful scale: https://playground.opendatalabs.xyz/

ODL’s research on data measurement and valuation provides tractable methods for identifying how different datasets influence model predictions — a prerequisite for accountability and auditability.

Applied projects demonstrate viability across domains:
- Federated, community-driven training with Flower Labs
- A decentralized robotics and egocentric data repository with Barbarika
- Behavioural and aesthetic forecasting with a Global 500 company
- Portable behavioural-credit signals for micro-lending with Haraka
- Privacy-preserving health and longevity data integration with a leading research group

ODL researchers contributed to standards such as Croissant (metadata schemas adopted in major ML venues) and led large-scale audits on consent collapse used in public reporting.
aiModel:
ODL does not build a single model; ODL builds the data layer that model builders rely on.
This includes:
- Provenance Infrastructure: Systems that document the full lifecycle of training data: collection, transformations, and integration into training pipelines.
- Data Measurement & Valuation Tools: Methods for estimating data influence on model behaviour, identifying high-value contributions, and detecting contamination or bias.
- Privacy-Preserving Data Use: Architectures that let institutions use sensitive data without centralising or exposing it: distributed training, secure enclaves, and cryptographic guarantees.
- Portable Data Formats & Metadata: Standards that maintain consent, provenance, and rights information as data moves across applications or institutions.
- Market & Incentive Prototypes: Mechanisms that explore how high-quality, rights-clear data can be exchanged or rewarded shifting incentives away from scale-first scraping.

All components are designed to integrate into existing AI workflows and to make data governance a practical part of model development rather than an afterthought.
barriers: Inconsistent data rights and portability laws create uncertainty for institutions trying to use data responsibly.
enablers: Partnerships with public institutions, civil society groups, and private companies to pilot provenance-aware, human-participatory data pipelines at scale.

title: AI-Powered Civic Education Resource
summary: VoteMate uses conversational AI and verified data sources to transform confusing ballots into personalized, trustworthy voting guidance, solving the problem that causes 53% of voters to skip races on their ballot or vote with uncertainty due to unrecognized candidates, inaccessible information, or lack of research time.
orgLocation: VoteMate is a 501(c)(3) headquartered in Los Angeles, CA with a distributed remote team supporting it.
beneficiaries: The 100+ million Americans who vote in local elections where information scarcity is most acute—especially working-class voters juggling multiple jobs (35% cite lack of time), communities without local news coverage (47% lack accessible information), and anyone facing down-ballot races featuring unfamiliar candidates for school boards, judges, city councils, and ballot measures that directly impact their daily lives but receive minimal media attention. We have focused on ballot measures, consitutional amendments, propositions and referrenda as these are an example of direct democracy - people voting on policy outcomes - and also tend to include long and confusing language that's challenging for voters to navigate and understand.
deploymentStage: Pilot / Limited Deployment: In use with a specific partner or limited user group.
evidence: We have conducted a limited proof-of-concept supporting voters before and during the November 2025 elections. The beta ran from 10/2/2025 through 11/4/2025 and we served a total of 7,652 users in all 50 states + DC. Efforts were targeted in Virginia, New Jersey, New York, California, and Texas. We do not yet have hard data on the imapct using VoteMate had on these voters (ie if they were more likely to vote, more informed about what was on their ballot, had more accurate information, etc) - we plan to study this in the coming months. We do have a lot of anecdotal feedback from users which is very positive and indicates that the product had the intended effects.
aiModel: For the beta, we deployed GPT-5 nano with a robust system instructions file which was designed, purpose-built, and extensively tested to shape the responses to fit the following criteria: fact-based, backed by verified sources, nonpartisan, unbiased, and useful specifically to voters making informed decisions. We also provided a grounding framework on voting and elections including guidance on how voting works in the US, what primary elections are vs. general elections, jurisdictional differences by state, etc.
barriers: (1) Getting the word out through marketing and other efforts (2) Public skepticism and build trust (3) Some technical limitations around collecting nationwide ballot data, which we're working towards (4) some financial limitations, which we're actively fundraising to address
enablers: (1) Reliable funding from foundations, individuals, etc. (2) Additional volunteers to support our efforts, especially folks with technical skills. VoteMate is an all-volunteer run organization so far.

title: Responsible AI Literacy for K–12 Students and Teachers
summary: A nationwide K–12 and educator-focused Ai literacy initiative that trains teachers and students to use Ai safely, ethically, and effectively while strengthening privacy, bias detection, and digital citizenship skills.
beneficiaries: K–12 students, teachers, instructional coaches, and Title I school communities that need practical, safe, and accessible Ai literacy education.
geoScope: Pilots in Texas and Florida, scalable nationwide through district adoption and state-level Ai literacy initiatives.
deploymentStage: Pilot / Limited Deployment: In use with a specific partner or limited user group.
evidence: Early pilots and development testing demonstrate that teachers can learn to identify bias in Ai outputs, protect student privacy, and construct effective instructional prompts in under 90 minutes. In district workshops, educators reported increased confidence and improved ability to review Ai-generated materials for safety and accuracy. Teachers and students using the stratified Ai literacy framework show improved digital citizenship, reduced misinformation risk, and more effective classroom use of district-approved tools.
aiModel: General-purpose large language models in controlled, district-approved environments (e.g., Claude & Chat GPT for development, Google/Microsoft closed systems for classroom use). Ai is used only as a drafting and idea-support tool. No student data is shared, and all outputs are reviewed by educators.
barriers: Uneven district policies on Ai use, limited teacher training, privacy compliance concerns, variable comfort with technology, and lack of clear state-level Ai literacy standards. Many low-resource districts lack the support needed to adopt safe Ai practices.
enablers: State-level Ai literacy requirements, district-approved Ai tool policies, funding for teacher professional development, and partnerships with public-interest Ai organizations. Access to standardized safety frameworks and district-led implementation support would significantly accelerate adoption.

title: DIY Render: Do-It-Yourself renderings in seconds. Crafted for the real estate industry.
summary: DIY Render is a web-based visual mediator that empowers users to generate marketing-ready real estate visualizations in seconds, bridging the gap between abstract concepts and final decisions.
beneficiaries: Realtors, Homeowners, General Contractors, and Interior Designers.
deploymentStage: Broadly Deployed: Widely available and in active use.
evidence:
Consider a renovation estimator who visits 10 homes in a week. Without visualization tools, they face a critical barrier: 83% of buyers cannot visualize a property as a future home without staging or visual aids, and 58% report being "disappointed" when homes don't match the polished look they see on TV design shows [1].

By using DIY Render to instantly align the property's appearance with these high expectations, the estimator directly addresses the "imagination gap" for those 8 clients who would otherwise hesitate. According to NAR data, 49% of seller's agents report that visualization and staging significantly reduce the time a project spends on the market [1].[1][2][3] Applying these metrics to the estimator's week, utilizing instant visualization can increase the likelihood of a sale (or signed contract) by ~50% by removing the primary friction point—time.

[1] National Association of Realtors (NAR), "2025 Profile of Home Staging," May 2025.[1][2][3][4]

[2] globenewswire.com: https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/05/06/3075133/0/en/NAR-Report-Reveals-Home-Staging-Boosts-Sale-Prices-and-Reduces-Time-on-Market.html

aiModel: DIY Render utilizes generative AI inpainting and generative fill technology. Users utilize a "brush" tool to highlight specific areas of a photograph (such as a floor, an empty corner, or unwanted furniture) and type a simple text prompt to generate realistic replacements or removals. Models include Google's Nano Banana Series & Multiple models used through Replicate.
barriers: Precision: As noted on the site, while conceptual changes are fast, "precise refinements" (such as replacing an object with a specific manufacturer's product SKU) remain difficult for the AI to execute perfectly compared to general conceptualization.
enablers: Commoditizing Design Intelligence. We need to optimize our models to the point where cost is negligible. This efficiency will allow us to offer an "architect-on-call" service to typically excluded markets, including affordable housing developers and low-income communities, transforming how they visualize and build their futures.

title: Getting dressed is one of humankind's most psychologically significant daily acts, yet it's overwhelmingly dismissed as frivolous vanity and/or simple utility. Research confirms what we wear directly influences how we think, feel, and behave (enclothed cognition) and how we are received by others. When people dress authentically, science shows measurable improvements in physical and mental wellbeing, confidence, and life satisfaction. Yet algorithmic feeds optimized for engagement, influence, and consumerism push people to chase micro-trends and fast fashion, disconnecting people from their authentic taste, preferences, and values which significantly contributes to rising mental health challenges, environmental devastation, and cultural homogenization. yourcore intervenes at the root: helping people reconnect with their authentic selves through something they already do each day, pick out their outfit of the day (or OOTD if you're chronically online like me). yourcore's AI assistant, Cori, operates as a mirror, not an oracle, reflecting users' patterns back to them rather than telling them what to wear, creating a proof-of-concept for ethical AI that amplifies human authenticity and individuality rather than extracting engagement, rewarding external validation, and homogenizing taste and style.
summary: yourcore is a fashion self-discovery app that uses Reflective AI to help users discover their authentic personal style through daily outfit documentation and journaling, creating cascading benefits for mental health, environmental sustainability, social connection, creative cognition, and resilience against algorithmic homogenization and cultural flattening — philosophy asks what makes us human; yourcore helps us remember.
domain: Mental Health & Wellbeing, Environmental Sustainability, Democracy Resilience/Resistance to Authoritarianism, Creative Cognition
beneficiaries:
Anyone navigating identity and self‑expression in a post‑COVID, algorithmically saturated world.
Gen Z (16–28): Entering the workforce after growing up on algorithmic feeds that shaped their taste before they could discover it themselves; 94% say they need guidance on what to wear to work and report outfit anxiety multiple times a month.
Millennials (29–44): Moving through postpartum, career pivots, divorce, and body changes with elevated appearance anxiety and strong links between mood, identity, and what they wear; 84% seek guidance on work attire.
Gen X (45–60): Reassessing identity at midlife after decades of dressing for roles; 70% want clearer cues on workplace dress and use clothing to negotiate stigma while defaulting to safe staples.
Boomers (60+): Redefining self‑expression in retirement and late career, prioritizing comfort (94%) yet still seeking guidance and using clothing to maintain social connection and visibility. 
Cross‑generational: 78% of workers across all four generations want guidance on what to wear and report outfit anxiety roughly seven times per month, in a context where post‑COVID body shifts, hybrid work, and social media have disrupted both dress codes and self‑concept.
geoScope: Initially United States (English-language launch), with global expansion potential. The psychological mechanisms — enclothed cognition, authentic self-expression, identity through dress — are cross-cultural. The environmental benefits of reduced overconsumption and resistance to algorithmic homogenization apply globally
deploymentStage: Pilot / Limited Deployment: In use with a specific partner or limited user group.
evidence:
Evidence of Positive Impact
yourcore's preliminary research (n=96) aligns almost point-for-point with what existing science says about outfit anxiety, identity disconnection, overconsumption, and the algorithmic homogenization that fuels all three. Cori turns out to be the antidote — solve for authenticity and the rest follows. Where conventional AI prescribes, Cori reflects. I call this framework "Reflective AI."
Mental Health & Outfit Anxiety Authentic self-expression is associated with higher life satisfaction, and randomized trials show that journaling produces measurable reductions in anxiety and other mental-health symptoms. In yourcore's early research (n=96), most respondents describe outfit stress as a "moderate, recurring problem" tied to not knowing what's appropriate and outfits that "never feel quite right," and say they want "an app that acts like a mirror, showing you things about you that you might have a hard time seeing yourself." Cori does exactly that by linking outfits to feelings over time and reflecting back the patterns users aren’t seeing themselves.
Identity & Physical Health Studies on identity concealment and authenticity link living incongruently with worse physical and mental health via chronic stress and immune effects. In yourcore's survey, the vast majority of respondents report experiencing a “positive feedback loop" at least once — wearing something that felt like them, noticing they showed up differently, and noticing others responded differently. Cori detects which outfits users tag as "felt like me," clusters their shared traits, and builds a personalized style language from those patterns so daily dressing becomes a repeated act of visible authenticity.
Creative Cognition & Brain Health Creative engagement is associated with better mental health, reduced mortality risk, and slower cognitive decline across hundreds of studies. yourcore respondents say they want playful experimentation with style but will only sustain it if it takes 2–5 minutes. Cori delivers this through daily style challenges (Cori Quests) and structured micro-journaling — quick photo plus a few taps, no blank page staring back. This makes daily creative practice accessible to those experimenting with style and people who've never journaled, and builds the habit by stacking on pre-existing routines through ease rather than effort — delivering the cognitive benefits of creativity without demanding extra time, tools, or talent.
Environmental Sustainability Clothing production has roughly doubled since 2000 while average garment use has fallen by about one-third — and research shows that even strong environmental values often don't translate into reduced fast-fashion purchasing. Several yourcore respondents already buy secondhand and explicitly ask for cost-per-wear and closet tracking to avoid regret purchases. Cori highlights wear counts, cost-per-wear, and regret patterns so behavior shifts through self-knowledge rather than guilt. The downstream effect: when people buy what they actually love because they know their taste, they keep it longer and buy less — sustainability through self-knowledge, not shame.
Social Connection & Democratic Resilience Research on dress and person perception shows that clothing is a core way people signal identity and find aligned communities, while work on authoritarian and far-right movements warns that enforced sameness and cultural homogenization erode democratic resilience. Conventional AI fashion recommenders are built to maximize similarity and convergence; in yourcore's survey, respondents favor a "discovery partner" over a "tells me what to wear" oracle by roughly six to one. Cori's Reflective AI architecture is intentionally mirror-not-oracle — using AI to magnify individual difference rather than erase it — so each day's outfit becomes a small act of authentic signaling instead of algorithmic groupthink.
Same pattern across all five: science identifies it, survey respondents confirm they're living it, Reflective AI addresses it — not by prescribing, but by reflecting.
aiModel:
yourcore is built on Lovable.dev. Cori, the AI assistant, uses Lovable's built-in LLM integration (Claude) with custom training on yourcore's Reflective AI framework — constrained to act as "mirror not oracle" by reflecting patterns from the user's own outfit, mood, and context logs rather than prescribing trends or pushing products. The system combines natural language interaction with lightweight analytics for wear counts, cost-per-wear, and pattern clustering from journaling data.
Cori’s future development includes the Authenticity Corpus — a to-be-documented, curated archive of 100+ interviews with artists, designers, psychologists, and everyday people exploring what authentic, creative self-expression means — to ground Cori's responses in human wisdom rather than engagement-optimized internet content. No fine-tuning on individual user data; all personalization comes from each user's own logs.
barriers: Perception: Fashion is often dismissed as frivolous, making it harder to secure funding, partnerships, and serious attention for a fashion psychology tool — even one with mental health, sustainability, and ethical AI implications. Solo non-technical founder: yourcore is currently built and maintained by one person using no-code/low-code tools (Lovable.dev). Scaling beyond MVP requires development resources, and navigating technical decisions without a technical co-founder creates risk and slows iteration. Go-to-market: Limited marketing budget means relying on organic growth, word-of-mouth, and earned media. Competing for attention against well-funded closet apps and fast-fashion platforms with massive ad spend is a challenge. Trust and privacy: Users may hesitate to share outfit photos and emotional data with an AI, even one designed with privacy in mind. Building trust requires transparency, clear data policies, and demonstrating the "mirror not oracle" difference. Behavior change is hard: Daily journaling requires habit formation. Even with micro-journaling and habit stacking, getting users to sustain engagement beyond the novelty phase is the core retention challenge all apps face.
enablers:
Open-source the Reflective AI framework. If "mirror not oracle" works for fashion, it could work for health apps, education platforms, financial tools — anywhere AI currently extracts attention instead of building self-knowledge. yourcore could become the proof-of-concept that spawns a design pattern. The right partner helps document it, test it across domains, and make it available to other builders who want an alternative to extraction architecture.
Partnerships with fashion and/or psychology researchers and sustainable fashion organizations. Academic partnerships would validate the mental health and sustainability claims with larger studies, while sustainable fashion orgs could help reach users who already care about overconsumption but lack tools beyond guilt-based messaging. Fashion therapy practitioners and researchers (like Dr. Dawnn Karen at Columbia and Professor Carolyn Mair at London College of Fashion) could provide clinical and academic credibility and referral pathways.
A cultural moment. Valentino sent "Fireflies" down the runway at Paris Fashion Week (s/s26) citing the same Pasolini philosophy yourcore is built on. The timing is there. One high-profile partnership — a sustainable fashion brand, a mental health organization, a celebrity who's publicly rejected algorithmic culture — could position yourcore as the tool for the authenticity movement that's already building. Not competing with fast fashion. Offering the exit ramp.
The Authenticity Corpus, funded and scaled. 100+ interviews with artists, designers, psychologists, and everyday people on what authentic self-expression actually means — then open it as an ethical AI training benchmark. Show that you can ground an LLM in curated human wisdom instead of engagement-optimized internet content. That's not just a feature for yourcore. That's infrastructure for the next generation of AI that actually serves people.
